Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/32148 (no longer applicable following this change).

issue_context.title: The KeyValuePair converter should cache the converters for TKey and TValue
issue_context.body:
As part of https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/2259, the KeyValuePair converter was identified as an area of potential perf improvement. Currently (and in 3.0\3.1) it re-enters the serializer to serialize `TKey` and `TValue` which is expensive because a Dictionary lookup occurs for each (to find the converter).

Instead, the converter should cache the converter. Caching is possible on the converter instance since the type is internal and there are no concerns about having an instance shared across different `JsonSerializerOptions` instances that may have different converters for `TKey` and `TValue`.

review_comments: The attribute does not seem to be effective on virtual methods.
So this should throw InvalidOperation but today we throw NullRef?

Yes, I think it should throw InvalidOperation.

I don't think we'll null ref in all cases. I just observed one in the converter for parameterized ctors due to the converter being passed a type that it can't convert (due to wrong assumptions about metadata on `state.Current.*` ). We may have the same/other issues with other converters.
I'm not following. If we want to invoke the ctor on KeyValuePair then we can just call it directly -- why the need for the indirection?

The problem is we have to duplicate all the logic for async (de)serialization (from the parameterized ctor converter) and make sure they stay in sync. The write side is relatively straightforward, but reading is more cumbersome - managing `state.Current.ObjectState`. `state.Current.PropertyState`, remembering previously parsed key/value ctor args (with `ArgumentState`) when we need to fetch more data etc.

If we had parameterized ctor support in v1 and didn't enforce that the payload have precisely 2 properties, one for the key and one for the value, we wouldn't have needed the KeyValuePair converter at all. The KeyValuePair has to exist only to do the property validation.
I see. We want to support Streams properly (meaning not using read-ahead) so we are leveraging the newly added ctor support to do that.
Yes, it's unused. It should have been removed in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/36322.

This converter type may come back depending on work in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/36785.
I have it this way so that two derived types don't need to override it and do nothing.
